query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small Ni dopant (on the order of a few weight percent) to a W–Cu composite via powder blending and high-temperature co-sintering will reduce phase separation and interfacial voids, leading to higher thermal conductivity under fusion-relevant heat and irradiation loads than the undoped W–Cu baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite with W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix, prepared by standard powder blending and sintering without additional alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor Ni dopant (1–3 wt%) into the W–Cu mixture, then perform high-temperature co-sintering under vacuum or inert atmosphere to promote Ni-assisted interfacial bonding and suppress phase separation.
generation.conditions: Heat-transfer and irradiation conditions typical of W–Cu joints in plasma-facing components, for example divertor and cooling channels in fusion reactors, with temperatures up to ~600–800 °C and moderate neutron/ion fluxes.
generation.structural_mediator: Ni dopant at W–Cu grain boundaries providing enhanced interfacial bonding and reduced interfacial energy.
generation.mechanism: Ni lowers interfacial energy, stabilizes the W–Cu interface, and mitigates vacancy agglomeration during high-temperature and irradiation, thereby decreasing void formation and preserving thermal transport paths.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped W–Cu composite, the Ni-doped material will exhibit reduced interfacial voids and measurably higher thermal conductivity (likely improved by at least several percent under extended heat and irradiation exposure).
generation.baseline: Undoped W–Cu composites fabricated by the same methods (powder blending and co-sintering) but without Ni addition.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness may depend on doping level and sintering parameters; extremely high temperatures or neutron fluxes may degrade the Ni-doped interface over very long service times, requiring further study.
generation.uncertainty: Precise magnitude of thermal conductivity improvements and long-term behavior under continuous high-dose irradiation are not fully validated by existing data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites, one undoped and one with ~2 wt% Ni, using identical powder blending and vacuum co-sintering conditions. Subject both sets to thermal cycling from room temperature to 800 °C under a representative neutron/ion fluence. After exposure, measure cross-sectional microstructure (SEM, TEM) for interfacial void fraction, evaluate thermal conductivity using a laser flash or steady-state method, and track any changes over irradiation time.
measurements: Thermal conductivity via laser flash or steady-state measurements
Microstructure characterization by SEM/TEM and EDS to examine Ni distribution and interfacial phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no reduction in interfacial void fraction is observed and if no improvement in thermal conductivity is measured in the Ni-doped composite after testing, the hypothesis is invalidated.

The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. Nuclear fusion-based power reactors require advancements with regard to high-temperature and plasma-facing materials in order to prevent degradation due to the exposure to high-temperature and high-energy neutron flux produced during deuterium-tritium fusion reactions. The severity of the service environment is expected to increase in upcoming fusion reactors with increased power ratings and those under transient scenarios. For instance, the heat load on the divertor, a key component of the tokamak design, , is expected to increase to 10 MW/m2 (steady state) and 20 MW/m2 (transient for 10 seconds). The inner and outer vertical targets of the divertor, where the kinetic energy of plasma particles is converted into heat, must withstand loads up to ~7–40 MJ/m2 and ~4–25 MJ/m2, respectively, under plasma disruption, . Therefore, unprecedented thermal, mechanical and physical characteristics are required for fusion reactor materials.

In this study, AZ91 magnesium-alloy-based metal matrix composites (MMCs) reinforced with 10 wt% of Al0.5CoCrFeNi2 high-entropy alloy (HEA) particles and SiC particles were prepared by a spark plasma sintering (SPS) process at 300 °C. The effects of reinforcements on the microstructure and mechanical properties of AZ91-based MMCs were studied. The results showed that AZ91–HEA composite consisted of α-Mg, Mg17Al12 and FCC phases. No interfacial reaction layer was observed between HEA particles and the Mg matrix. After adding HEA into AZ91, the compressive yield strength (C.Y.S) of the AZ91–HEA composite increased by 17% without degradation of failure strain. In addition, the increment in C.Y.S brought by HEA was comparable to that contributed by commonly used SiC reinforcement (15%). A relatively low porosity in the composite and enhanced interfacial bonding between the α-Mg matrix and HEA particles make HEA a potential reinforcement material in MMCs.
